questions.q: A research platform runs an orchestrator with 12 parallel worker agents. Workers duplicate each other's searches. The architectural fix is:
opts: More workers
Orchestrator assigns explicit, disjoint subtask boundaries and a shared task ledger workers consult
Let workers negotiate freely
Reduce to one worker
questions.exp: Duplication between workers is a coordination failure, not a capability one. Each worker is reasoning sensibly in isolation and arriving at the same obvious next search, because nothing tells it what the others are doing. The fix is to make the division explicit: the orchestrator assigns disjoint boundaries, and a shared ledger lets workers see what has already been claimed. Adding workers multiplies the duplication. Letting them negotiate re-couples the contexts that isolation was meant to separate, which costs the parallelism you paid for.
why: More workers multiplies the duplication rather than resolving it, since nothing has changed about how work is divided.
Correct. Explicit disjoint subtask boundaries plus a shared ledger, so each worker knows what is already claimed.
Free negotiation re-couples the contexts that isolation existed to separate, giving back the parallelism you paid for.
One worker eliminates duplication by eliminating parallelism, which discards the reason for the design.

questions.q: When an orchestrator delegates to workers, what should flow back?
opts: Each worker's full transcript
Compact structured results (findings, citations, confidence) against the assigned subtask contract
Nothing until the end
Raw tool logs
questions.exp: Compact structured results against the subtask contract: findings, citations, and a confidence signal. The orchestrator needs enough to decide what happens next, not a replay of how the worker got there - and returning full transcripts is what makes fan-out architectures collapse under their own context, since the orchestrator pays for every intermediate step of every worker. Confidence matters as much as content, because it tells the orchestrator which findings need corroboration before they are acted on.
why: A full transcript floods the orchestrator with every intermediate step, which is what makes fan-out designs collapse under their own context.
Correct. Compact structured results against the assigned contract - findings, citations and confidence - so the orchestrator can decide next steps.
Withholding everything until the end removes the orchestrator's ability to redirect a worker that has gone off track.
Raw logs are the least distilled form available and carry the same context problem as full transcripts.

questions.q: You must choose between one agent with 40 tools vs. a router to 4 specialist agents with ~10 tools each. Specialists win mainly because:
opts: More total compute
Smaller focused tool sets and prompts reduce selection errors and context bloat per query
It looks better in diagrams
Routers are free
questions.exp: Specialists win because both the prompt and the tool set shrink to what one category actually needs. Tool selection degrades as the surface grows - forty tools means more near-miss options that all look plausible - and every one of them costs context on every request whether or not it is relevant. A specialist carries ten. The routing call is the overhead you accept in exchange, and it is usually trivial next to what it saves in both accuracy and tokens.
why: Total compute is not the mechanism. The gain comes from a smaller decision space and less context per request.
Correct. Smaller focused tool sets and prompts reduce selection errors and context bloat on every query.
Architecture diagrams are not a design criterion, and the benefit here is measurable rather than presentational.
Routing costs a classification call. It is cheap relative to the saving, but it is not free.

questions.q: A long-horizon agent must survive process restarts mid-task. Professional-grade design:
opts: Keep state only in the context window
Externalize state: durable task ledger/checkpoints so any run can resume from last known-good step
Never restart
Rerun from scratch each time
questions.exp: State that only exists in the context window dies with the process. Externalising it - a durable task ledger with checkpoints - lets any run resume from the last known-good step, which is what makes a long-horizon agent operationally viable rather than merely impressive when nothing goes wrong. The design question worth asking early is what a restart costs: if the answer is everything, the system is one deployment or one crash away from losing hours of work, and restarts are not rare events.
why: Context-window state is lost the moment the process ends, which makes every restart a total loss.
Correct. Externalised state with checkpoints lets any run resume from the last known-good step.
Restarts are not optional. Deployments, crashes and scaling events all cause them.
Rerunning from scratch discards completed work and repeats its cost every time.

questions.q: Which task profile justifies multi-agent parallelization despite ~15x token cost?
opts: Simple FAQ answering
Breadth-heavy research where independent subtopics can be explored simultaneously and synthesized
Formatting a document
Single API lookup
questions.exp: Breadth-heavy research is the profile that earns the multiple: independent subtopics can be explored at once and synthesised at the end, so the wall-clock gain is real and the isolation keeps each worker's context focused. The token cost is genuinely large - each worker re-establishes its own context - which is exactly why the justification has to be specific rather than general. Simple lookups, formatting and single API calls have no independent branches to explore, so parallelism multiplies cost and buys nothing.
why: A single FAQ answer has no independent branches to explore, so parallelism multiplies cost for no gain.
Correct. Breadth-heavy research with independent subtopics explored simultaneously and synthesised at the end.
Formatting is a single deterministic transformation with nothing to parallelise.
A single lookup is one call. Parallelising it produces the same answer several times over.

questions.q: An agent's tool starts returning subtly wrong data (not errors). The strongest defense layer is:
opts: Hope the model notices
Validation checks/invariants on tool outputs in code, with anomalies surfaced to the agent or halting the pipeline
Longer prompts
Retrying the same call
questions.exp: Wrong-but-valid data is the hardest failure to catch, because nothing signals it: no exception, no error code, just plausible values that are incorrect. The defence has to be in code - invariants and validation checks on tool outputs, with anomalies either surfaced to the agent or halting the pipeline. Hoping the model notices places the check inside the same reasoning that will consume the bad value, which is precisely where it is least likely to fire. Retrying returns the same wrong data reliably.
why: The model has no independent reference to compare against, and the wrong value is exactly what it will reason from.
Correct. Invariants and validation on tool outputs in code, with anomalies surfaced or the pipeline halted.
More instruction text does not give the model a way to detect that a plausible value is wrong.
A deterministic tool returns the same wrong data on retry, so this confirms the failure rather than resolving it.

questions.q: Design a fallback chain for a customer-facing agent when the primary model times out:
opts: Show an error page
Retry with backoff → fallback model tier → cached/templated response → human handoff, with each step logged
Infinite retries
Switch to a random provider silently
questions.exp: Each rung handles a different failure and degrades a little further: backoff for transients, a fallback tier when the primary is unavailable, a cached or templated response when models are unreachable, and human handoff when nothing automated will do. Logging each step is what makes the chain debuggable afterwards, and it is the part most often left out. Note that silently switching providers is worse than an error - the user gets an answer of unknown provenance, and nobody knows which system produced it.
why: An error page discards every intermediate option, most of which would have produced a usable answer.
Correct. Backoff, then a fallback tier, then a cached or templated response, then human handoff - each step logged.
Unbounded retries hang the request and hammer a service already failing, with no path to a fallback.
Silent provider switching produces an answer of unknown provenance that nobody can trace or reason about.

questions.q: A batch agent pipeline fails at step 7 of 10 nightly. Rerunning all 10 steps doubles cost. Fix:
opts: Accept the cost
Idempotent steps with checkpointed intermediate artifacts so reruns resume at the failure point
Delete step 7
Run weekly instead
questions.exp: Checkpoint each step's output and make the steps idempotent, so a rerun resumes at the failure rather than repeating the nine steps that already worked. Idempotency is the part that makes it safe: without it, resuming risks doing something twice, which for anything with side effects is worse than the original failure. The pattern generalises to any long pipeline - persisted intermediate artifacts convert a total rerun into a partial one, and the saving grows with pipeline length.
why: Accepting the cost pays for nine successful steps again every night, indefinitely.
Correct. Idempotent steps with checkpointed artifacts, so a rerun resumes at the failure point rather than the beginning.
Removing the failing step removes whatever it produced, which the remaining steps presumably depend on.
Running less often reduces how many times you pay the cost without addressing why the rerun is total.

questions.q: How should an agent handle ambiguous instructions in a high-stakes workflow?
opts: Guess confidently
Detect ambiguity and ask for clarification or route to a human rather than acting on assumptions
Always pick the cheaper interpretation
Refuse everything
questions.exp: Detect the ambiguity and ask, or route to a human. In a high-stakes workflow a confident guess is the worst outcome available: it produces a decisive action on an interpretation nobody validated, and the error is invisible because the output looks like every other successful run. Note the counterweight - an agent that asks about everything is unusable, so the skill is calibrating when ambiguity actually changes the outcome. Defaulting to the cheaper reading is a decision rule that has nothing to do with which reading is correct.
why: A confident guess produces decisive action on an unvalidated interpretation, and nothing in the output reveals it.
Correct. Detect the ambiguity and ask, or route to a human, rather than acting on an assumption.
Cost is unrelated to correctness. This picks an interpretation by price rather than by evidence.
Refusing everything makes the agent useless. The skill is calibrating when ambiguity genuinely matters.

questions.q: A pipeline uses Opus-class for every step including trivial formatting. The optimization is:
opts: Nothing — consistency matters most
Model tiering: route each step to the cheapest model that meets its quality bar, verified by evals
Drop quality checks
Remove formatting steps
questions.exp: Route each step to the cheapest model that clears its quality bar, and verify that bar with evals rather than intuition. Most pipelines are mostly simple steps, so tiering captures a large saving without touching the work that genuinely needed capability - and the eval is what turns this from a guess into a decision you can defend when someone asks why quality would hold. Consistency is a real value but a weak argument here, since it is consistency of cost rather than of output.
why: Consistency of model is not consistency of output, and it pays a premium on every trivial step.
Correct. Route each step to the cheapest model meeting its quality bar, with evals verifying the bar holds.
Removing quality checks trades a measurable saving for an unmeasurable risk.
Formatting steps exist because something needs formatting. Deleting them removes output the pipeline requires.

questions.q: Which lever cuts cost the most for an agent with a large stable system prompt + tools called 100k times/day?
opts: Shorter variable names
Prompt caching of the stable prefix
More parallelism
Lower max_tokens by 10
questions.exp: Cache the stable prefix. A large system prompt and tool set are byte-identical on every one of those calls and are billed in full each time without caching; cached reads cost roughly a tenth of the base input rate, which at that volume dwarfs every other lever available. The requirement is ordering, since caching is a prefix match: stable content first, anything volatile after the last breakpoint. Get that wrong and the cache silently never hits - no error, just full price forever.
why: Variable naming is invisible to the API. Only prompt content is billed.
Correct. Caching the stable prefix, which is billed in full on every call otherwise and dominates cost at this volume.
Parallelism affects throughput and rate limits rather than the cost of each call.
Ten tokens against a large prompt sent 100,000 times is a rounding error.

questions.q: Latency-sensitive interactive step + quality-sensitive back-office step. Strategy?
opts: Same model for both
Fast model (streaming) for interactive; stronger model, possibly with extended thinking, for the async step
Strongest model for both
Fastest model for both
questions.exp: Match the model to what each step is actually constrained by. The interactive step is bounded by perceived latency, so a fast model with streaming wins - the user sees progress immediately and total completion time matters less than time to first token. The back-office step has no one waiting, so capability and reasoning effort are worth their cost there. Using one model for both means one of the two constraints goes unserved: either the interactive step feels slow or the async step is weaker than it needed to be.
why: One model cannot be optimal for both, so whichever you choose leaves one constraint unserved.
Correct. A fast streaming model where latency is felt, a stronger model with more reasoning where accuracy matters and nobody waits.
The strongest model everywhere makes the interactive step feel slow and pays a premium where speed was the requirement.
The fastest model everywhere under-serves the quality-sensitive step, where there was no latency constraint to satisfy.

questions.q: How should you tune how much Claude reasons on a given class of task?
opts: Always run at the maximum setting
Empirically — set reasoning effort per task class from evals showing where added reasoning actually improves outcomes
Leave it at the default and never revisit it
Turn reasoning off everywhere to save tokens
questions.exp: Set reasoning effort per task class from evidence. Effort is a paid dial and only some workloads convert it into better outcomes - on well-specified extraction or classification it adds tokens and latency for no measurable gain, while on multi-step analysis it is where the accuracy comes from. Running everything at maximum is expensive and can produce overthinking on simple tasks; turning it off everywhere costs you the hard cases. Leaving the default untouched forever means never learning which of your task classes are which.
why: Maximum everywhere is expensive and can produce overthinking on simple tasks that never needed it.
Correct. Set effort per task class from evals showing where added reasoning actually improves the outcome.
The default is a reasonable starting point rather than a tuned answer, and never revisiting it leaves the saving unclaimed.
Turning reasoning off globally saves tokens on easy tasks by degrading the hard ones that justified the model.

questions.q: Before swapping a prompt in a production agent, you should:
opts: Ship it — it reads better
Run it against a versioned eval suite of representative and edge cases, comparing to the incumbent
Ask one colleague
Test in production
questions.exp: Run the candidate against a versioned eval suite of representative and edge cases and compare it against the incumbent. The comparison is what makes it evidence rather than an impression - and it catches the failure informal review always misses, where a change fixes one issue while introducing another. Shipping because it reads better substitutes aesthetics for measurement, and a prompt that reads well is not reliably one that performs well. Testing in production means your users are the regression suite.
why: How a prompt reads to a person is weakly related to how it performs, and this substitutes aesthetics for measurement.
Correct. Run it against a versioned eval suite covering representative and edge cases, compared against the incumbent.
One colleague's reaction is a sample of one opinion rather than evidence about behaviour across cases.
Testing in production makes your users the regression suite, and you learn from failures they experienced.

questions.q: What belongs in an agent observability stack?
opts: Only error counts
Traces of each step (tool calls, inputs/outputs, tokens, latency), outcome metrics, and sampled human review of transcripts
CPU temperature
Screenshots
questions.exp: You need three layers, because each answers a different question. Step-level traces - tool calls, inputs and outputs, tokens, latency - tell you what happened inside a run. Outcome metrics tell you whether runs are succeeding, which traces alone do not. Sampled human review of transcripts catches the quality problems no automated metric is watching for, which is how silent degradation gets found. Error counts alone are the common gap: they detect crashes and are blind to a system that runs perfectly and answers badly.
why: Error counts detect crashes and are blind to a system that runs without failing and answers badly.
Correct. Step-level traces, outcome metrics, and sampled human review - each catching failures the others miss.
Infrastructure telemetry is unrelated to whether the agent's reasoning and outputs are sound.
Screenshots capture appearance rather than the decisions, tool calls and outcomes that need observing.

questions.q: An LLM-as-judge eval disagrees with human raters 40% of the time. You should:
opts: Trust the judge — it's cheaper
Calibrate: refine the judge rubric against human-labeled examples until agreement is acceptable, or keep humans for that axis
Delete the eval
Average the two
questions.exp: Forty percent disagreement means the judge is not measuring what you care about, so calibrate it: refine the rubric against human-labelled examples until agreement is acceptable, or keep humans for that axis. A judge is only as good as its rubric, and vague criteria produce impressions that vary run to run. Trusting it because it is cheaper optimises confidently against the wrong target. Averaging a calibrated signal with an uncalibrated one produces a number nobody can interpret.
why: Cost is irrelevant if the measurement is wrong. Cheap disagreement with your actual quality bar is worse than no metric.
Correct. Calibrate the rubric against human-labelled examples until agreement is acceptable, or keep humans on that axis.
Deleting the eval removes the measurement rather than fixing it, leaving you with no signal at all.
Averaging a calibrated signal with an uncalibrated one yields a number that means nothing in particular.

questions.q: Production metrics show quality drift after a model version update. First professional response:
opts: Panic rollback of everything
Rerun the eval suite on the new version, identify failing segments, then patch prompts or pin/route models accordingly
Ignore three weeks
Blame users
questions.exp: Rerun the eval suite on the new version and find out which segments regressed. That converts a vague sense of drift into a specific list you can act on - patch the affected prompts, or pin and route those cases to the previous version while you fix them. The suite is what makes a targeted response possible; without it the only options are rolling everything back or waiting. Note that some drift is expected on any version change, which is exactly why prompts written for one model need re-tuning for the next.
why: A blanket rollback discards genuine improvements and does not tell you what actually regressed.
Correct. Rerun the eval suite, identify the failing segments, then patch prompts or pin and route accordingly.
Waiting leaves users with degraded output while the cause remains undiagnosed.
Attribution does not restore quality, and the regression is in the system rather than in how it is used.

questions.q: An agent has email-send and file-delete tools. Governance requires:
opts: Nothing special
Least-privilege scoping, human approval gates for irreversible actions, and immutable audit logs of every action
A faster model
Disabling logging for privacy
questions.exp: Three controls, each covering something the others do not. Least-privilege scoping bounds what the tools can reach at all. Approval gates on irreversible actions catch the individual operation that should not happen. Immutable audit logs answer what did happen afterwards, which matters for both incident response and accountability. Note that logging is a governance requirement rather than a privacy problem - the right answer to sensitive content in logs is redaction and access control, not turning the logs off.
why: Irreversible external actions are exactly the case that needs governance, and the absence of controls is the risk.
Correct. Least-privilege scoping, approval gates on irreversible actions, and immutable audit logs.
Model capability is not a control. A faster model performs the wrong action sooner.
Disabling logging removes accountability. Sensitive content in logs is handled by redaction and access control instead.

questions.q: Your agent browses arbitrary web content, then can call internal tools. Biggest threat to design against?
opts: Slow pages
Prompt injection from fetched content steering internal tool calls — isolate/sanitize content, restrict tool access in browsing contexts
Image-heavy pages
Cookie banners
questions.exp: The threat is prompt injection: fetched content carrying text designed to steer the agent's internal tool calls. The combination is what makes it serious - browsing alone is low-risk, internal tools alone are controlled, and joining them creates a path from attacker-controlled text to privileged action. Isolate and sanitise fetched content, and restrict which tools are reachable while browsing. The defence has to be structural, because the model cannot reliably distinguish instructions it should follow from instructions embedded in text it was asked to read.
why: Latency is an experience concern rather than a security one, and slow pages harm nobody's data.
Correct. Injection from fetched content steering internal tool calls - isolate the content and restrict tool access while browsing.
Image-heavy pages affect cost and processing time rather than creating a path to privileged action.
Consent banners are noise in the content. They are not a route to your internal systems.

questions.q: Customer PII flows through an agent pipeline. Professional handling includes:
opts: Logging everything verbatim forever
Data minimization, redaction/masking before model calls where feasible, retention policies, and access controls on traces
Emailing logs weekly
Avoiding documentation
questions.exp: Minimise what is collected, redact or mask before model calls where the task allows, set retention limits, and control access to traces. That last one is the piece most often missed: observability data contains everything the agent saw, so a trace store is a copy of your sensitive data with different access controls than the system it came from. Logging everything verbatim forever is the specific failure - it converts a transient processing step into a permanent record with a much larger exposure surface.
why: Verbatim permanent logging turns a transient processing step into an indefinite record with a much larger exposure surface.
Correct. Minimisation, redaction before model calls where feasible, retention limits, and access controls on traces.
Emailing logs distributes sensitive data into an uncontrolled channel, which multiplies the exposure.
Documentation is what makes handling reviewable and defensible. Avoiding it hides the problem rather than reducing it.

questions.q: Who should be able to modify a production agent's system prompt?
opts: Anyone, anytime
Authorized roles via change control (review + eval gate + versioned deploy), like any production code change
The model itself freely
Nobody ever
questions.exp: The system prompt is production configuration that determines behaviour, so it belongs under the same change control as code: authorised roles, review, an eval gate, and a versioned deploy. Anything less means behaviour can change with no record and no way to attribute a regression. Note that both extremes fail - unrestricted editing pushes untested changes to every user at once, and freezing it entirely prevents the improvements that evals exist to validate. Letting the model edit its own instructions removes the boundary altogether.
why: Unrestricted editing pushes untested behaviour changes to every user with no record and no way to attribute a regression.
Correct. Authorised roles via change control - review, eval gate, versioned deploy - exactly like production code.
An agent editing its own instructions removes the boundary that governs its behaviour.
Freezing it prevents the improvements that the eval process exists to validate.

questions.q: An agent completed '95% of the task' then errored. Users got nothing. Improvement?
opts: Bigger model
Design for partial delivery: stream/persist intermediate results so completed work survives failures
Faster CPUs
Retry the whole task
questions.exp: Design for partial delivery. Streaming or persisting intermediate results means a late failure still hands over the work already done, which converts a total loss into a partial success - and on long-running tasks that is the difference between a frustrating system and an unusable one. A larger model does not change what happens when a run fails at the end, and retrying the whole task repeats everything that already succeeded, paying for it twice while the same failure may well recur.
why: Capability does not change what happens when a run fails late. The completed work is still discarded.
Correct. Stream or persist intermediate results so completed work survives a late failure.
Infrastructure speed is unrelated to whether partial results are preserved when a run fails.
Retrying the whole task repeats everything that already succeeded and may hit the same failure again.

questions.q: You're scaling from 1 to 50 concurrent agent sessions sharing tools and rate limits. Key addition:
opts: Nothing changes
Central concurrency/rate management: queues, per-session budgets, and backpressure so sessions degrade fairly
50 API keys
Larger prompts
questions.exp: Shared limits mean sessions now compete, so the architecture needs something that arbitrates: queues, per-session budgets, and backpressure so load sheds fairly instead of one runaway session starving the rest. Without it the failure mode is unfair rather than merely slow - a single session in a retry loop can consume the shared quota and degrade forty-nine others. Extra API keys attempt to evade limits rather than manage demand, which is a terms problem as well as an ineffective one.
why: Fifty sessions sharing one quota is a materially different system. A single runaway session can starve the rest.
Correct. Queues, per-session budgets and backpressure, so load sheds fairly rather than one session starving the others.
Multiple keys attempt to evade limits rather than manage demand, which is a terms problem as well as ineffective.
Prompt size affects cost per call rather than how contention between concurrent sessions is arbitrated.

questions.q: The best eval set for a support agent is built from:
opts: Synthetic easy questions only
Representative real cases plus curated hard/edge cases and known past failures, refreshed over time
One demo transcript
Marketing copy
questions.exp: Real cases keep the set representative, curated hard and edge cases keep it discriminating, and known past failures stop old bugs coming back. Refreshing it matters as much as building it: production traffic drifts, and a set that no longer reflects what users ask will look healthy while quality falls. That is the failure mode worth naming - a stale eval suite does not report that it is stale, it just keeps passing. Synthetic easy questions measure the path that was never going to fail.
why: Easy synthetic questions measure the path that was never at risk, so the suite passes while real failures go unseen.
Correct. Representative real cases plus curated hard cases and known past failures, refreshed as traffic drifts.
One transcript is a single sample and cannot represent the distribution of real support conversations.
Marketing copy is neither a representative input nor a case with a checkable correct answer.

questions.q: An orchestrator spawns workers whose combined output no longer fits in its own context. The right response is:
opts: Increase the orchestrator's context window and continue
Have workers return bounded, schema-constrained summaries, and synthesize in stages if needed
Reduce the number of workers until it fits
Drop the results that arrive last
questions.exp: Bound what workers return rather than expanding what the orchestrator can hold. Schema-constrained summaries cap each contribution at a known size, and staged synthesis handles the case where even bounded summaries exceed the window - combine in groups, then combine the combinations. Enlarging the orchestrator's window buys headroom without changing the growth, so the same problem returns one worker later. Reducing worker count trades away the parallelism you built the fleet for, and dropping late results silently loses work you already paid for.
why: A larger window delays the same problem rather than solving it, since output still grows with worker count.
Correct. Bounded, schema-constrained summaries from each worker, synthesised in stages when needed.
Cutting workers gives back the parallelism that justified the design, to avoid a problem bounding output would fix.
Discarding late results silently loses completed work and makes the output depend on arrival timing.

questions.q: A multi-agent design costs many times a single-agent one. That is justified when:
opts: The team prefers agents
Parallel exploration measurably improves outcomes enough to warrant the token multiple
The vendor promotes it
The task is long
questions.exp: The justification has to be measured. Multi-agent designs cost several times a single agent because every worker re-establishes its own context, so the question is whether parallel exploration improves outcomes enough to warrant that multiple on your workload. Team preference, vendor promotion and task duration are all reasons someone might reach for it, and none of them is evidence. Long tasks in particular are a trap: length suggests effort rather than parallelism, and a long sequential task gains nothing from fan-out.
why: Preference is not evidence. Wanting the pattern says nothing about whether it improves outcomes here.
Correct. When parallel exploration measurably improves outcomes enough to justify the token multiple.
Vendor promotion describes what a pattern can do rather than whether your workload benefits from it.
Length suggests effort rather than parallelism. A long sequential task gains nothing from fan-out.

questions.q: Subagents in a fleet should generally not coordinate directly with each other because:
opts: It is technically impossible
Cross-talk destroys the context isolation and parallelism that made the design worthwhile
It is slower to send messages
The protocol forbids it
questions.exp: Direct coordination undoes the two properties that made the design worth its cost. Isolation goes first: once subagents exchange context, each one carries the others' material and the context saving disappears. Parallelism follows, because agents waiting on each other serialise. Route coordination through the orchestrator, which holds the shared state deliberately and in a bounded form. Note this is a default rather than an absolute - some designs do need agent-to-agent messaging, and the point is to pay for it knowingly.
why: It is technically possible, which is exactly why the discipline matters. The constraint is architectural rather than mechanical.
Correct. Cross-talk destroys the context isolation and parallelism that justified the fleet in the first place.
Latency is a minor consideration next to losing isolation and serialising work that was meant to run in parallel.
Nothing prohibits it. This is a design judgement about preserving the benefits you paid for.

questions.q: The orchestrator's context in a large fleet should contain:
opts: Every subagent's full transcript
Compact structured results and the state needed to decide next steps
Only the original user request
The full contents of every tool response
questions.exp: Compact structured results plus whatever state the next decision needs - no more. The orchestrator's job is routing and synthesis, and it needs conclusions rather than the reasoning that produced them. Carrying full transcripts is what makes a fleet collapse under its own context, since the orchestrator ends up holding every worker's intermediate step. The opposite failure is real too: keeping only the original request leaves it unable to decide anything, because it has no idea what has been established so far.
why: Full transcripts put every worker's intermediate reasoning into one context, which is what makes fleets collapse.
Correct. Compact structured results plus the state needed to decide next steps - conclusions rather than reasoning.
The original request alone leaves the orchestrator unable to decide anything, since it knows nothing of what workers found.
Full tool responses are the least distilled form available and carry the same problem as transcripts.

questions.q: A fleet's aggregate token usage grows faster than its task volume. The first thing to examine is:
opts: Whether users are asking harder questions
Whether agents are retrying, looping, or re-reading context they already have
Whether the model changed
Whether logging is too verbose
questions.exp: Superlinear growth against volume means something is being repeated rather than something being harder. Retries, loops, and agents re-reading context they already hold are the usual causes, and they are all invisible in an aggregate bill - which is why the first move is to look at per-run traces rather than at totals. Harder questions and a model change would raise cost roughly in proportion to volume; the disproportion is the clue that work is being done more than once.
why: Harder questions raise cost roughly in proportion to volume. The disproportion points at repeated work instead.
Correct. Retries, loops and agents re-reading context they already hold - work being done more than once.
A model change shifts the per-token rate. It does not make usage grow faster than task volume.
Logging volume affects your logging costs rather than tokens consumed by the model.

questions.q: Your fallback chain silently serves answers from a weaker model during an outage. The design problem is:
opts: The weaker model costs less, so quality is being over-paid for
Users and downstream systems cannot tell a degraded answer from a normal one, so they trust it equally
Fallbacks should never be used in production
The chain should retry the primary model indefinitely instead
questions.exp: Graceful degradation is only graceful if the consumer knows it happened. An answer served from a fallback tier may be perfectly usable, or may be materially weaker on exactly the hard cases that matter - and a caller with no signal treats both identically, which is how a quiet outage becomes a quality incident nobody attributes correctly. Surface which tier answered: in the response metadata for downstream systems, and visibly where a person is relying on it for a consequential decision. It also makes the outage measurable afterwards, since fallback rate becomes a metric rather than an inference.
why: Cost is not the issue. A cheaper answer that nobody knows is a fallback is the problem, whatever it cost.
Correct. Without a signal, consumers trust a degraded answer exactly as much as a normal one.
Fallbacks are the right pattern. The gap is that the degradation is invisible, not that it exists.
Indefinite retry removes the fallback's purpose and leaves users waiting through the entire outage.

questions.q: A nightly ten-step pipeline fails at step seven. The most efficient recovery is:
opts: Rerun all ten steps
Resume from step seven using persisted outputs of the earlier steps
Skip step seven
Run the pipeline twice nightly
questions.exp: Resume from the failure using the persisted outputs of the earlier steps. Six successful steps have already been paid for, and rerunning them costs the same again for a guaranteed identical result. This requires the earlier outputs to be durable and the steps to be safely re-enterable, which is a design decision worth making before you need it. Skipping the failing step removes whatever it produced, and running twice nightly doubles the cost of a pipeline that is already failing.
why: Rerunning all ten repeats six successful steps at full cost for a guaranteed identical result.
Correct. Resume from the failure point using the persisted outputs of the steps that already succeeded.
Skipping the step removes its output, which the later steps presumably depend on.
Running more often multiplies the cost of a pipeline that is already failing partway through.

questions.q: A downstream dependency degrades intermittently under load. The right agent-side behavior is:
opts: Retry immediately and continuously
Backoff with jitter, a retry ceiling, and a defined fallback when the ceiling is hit
Fail the entire run on first error
Ignore the errors and continue
questions.exp: Backoff with jitter, a retry ceiling, and a defined fallback when the ceiling is hit. Each part matters: backoff gives the dependency room to recover, jitter stops your clients retrying in lockstep and extending the overload, the ceiling bounds how long you spend trying, and the fallback decides what happens when trying has failed. Immediate continuous retry is the worst option because it adds load to something already struggling. Failing the run on the first error discards work over a condition that is transient by definition.
why: Immediate continuous retry adds load to a dependency already failing, which extends the degradation.
Correct. Backoff with jitter, a retry ceiling, and a defined fallback when the ceiling is reached.
Failing the whole run on the first error discards work over a condition that is transient by definition.
Ignoring errors means continuing with missing or wrong data, which produces confidently incorrect output.

questions.q: Distinguishing recoverable from unrecoverable failures matters because:
opts: It reduces token cost
Retrying an unrecoverable failure burns budget and delays surfacing a problem that needs a human
It makes logs shorter
The API requires the distinction
questions.exp: The two need opposite responses. Retrying a recoverable failure is how it resolves; retrying an unrecoverable one burns budget and, worse, delays surfacing a problem that needs a person - a malformed request or a revoked credential will fail identically forever. Treating everything as retryable makes an agent look busy while getting nowhere, which is harder to spot than an outright failure. The classification also gives you a place to hang the escalation path.
why: Cost is a consequence rather than the reason. The point is that retrying an unrecoverable failure never succeeds.
Correct. Retrying an unrecoverable failure burns budget and delays surfacing a problem that needs human attention.
Log volume is incidental. The distinction is about which response is appropriate.
Nothing in the API requires it. It is a design decision about how to respond to different failures.

questions.q: A production agent silently produces lower-quality output after a dependency schema change. This was missed because:
opts: The model degraded
There was no outcome monitoring — only crash-level alerting
The prompt was too short
Users did not complain loudly enough
questions.exp: Crash-level alerting only sees failures. A schema change that leaves the system running while degrading its output produces no errors at all, so nothing fires - and that is the general shape of the most expensive production problems in agent systems: they succeed at doing the wrong thing. Outcome monitoring is what catches it, because it measures whether runs are producing good results rather than whether they completed. Waiting for complaints means the users are the monitoring, and most of them will not report it.
why: The model is unchanged. The input changed shape, which the system handled without erroring.
Correct. Only crash-level alerting was in place, so a system that ran successfully while degrading raised nothing.
Prompt length is unrelated to a dependency changing the shape of what it returns.
Relying on complaints makes users the monitoring, and most degradation is never reported.

questions.q: An interactive step must feel fast and an overnight step must be accurate. The right strategy is:
opts: The same model for both
A fast model with streaming for the interactive step; a stronger model, and more reasoning effort, for the async step
The strongest model for both
The fastest model for both
questions.exp: Match each step to its binding constraint. The interactive step is bounded by perceived latency, so a fast model with streaming wins - the user sees progress immediately, and time to first token matters more than total duration. The overnight step has nobody waiting, so capability and reasoning effort convert directly into quality at no experienced cost. One model for both necessarily under-serves one of them, and which one depends only on which model you picked.
why: A single model cannot satisfy both constraints, so whichever you pick leaves one of them unserved.
Correct. A fast streaming model where latency is felt, a stronger model with more reasoning effort where accuracy matters.
The strongest model everywhere makes the interactive step feel slow while paying a premium for it.
The fastest model everywhere under-serves the accuracy-sensitive step that had no latency constraint.

questions.q: Latency is dominated by a large fixed prompt resent on every call. The most effective change is:
opts: Shorten variable user input
Cache the stable prefix so repeated content is not reprocessed each time
Lower max_tokens
Add more concurrency
questions.exp: Cache the stable prefix. A large fixed prompt is reprocessed on every call without caching, and that processing is the latency you are seeing - a cached prefix skips it, which improves time to first token as well as cost. The ordering requirement is what makes it work: caching is a prefix match, so the stable content must come first and anything volatile must follow the last breakpoint. Shortening the variable input addresses the small part, and lowering the output ceiling truncates responses rather than speeding up the prefix.
why: The variable input is the small part. The fixed prompt is what dominates both cost and processing time.
Correct. Caching the stable prefix skips reprocessing it on every call, improving both latency and cost.
Lowering the output ceiling truncates responses rather than reducing the time spent on the prompt.
Concurrency raises throughput without reducing the latency of any individual call.

questions.q: Deciding whether to move a step to a cheaper model, the deciding evidence should be:
opts: The price difference alone
An eval on representative production cases showing quality holds
A colleague's experience on a different task
The newest model available
questions.exp: Run an eval on representative production cases and check that quality holds. That is the only evidence that answers the actual question - is this model good enough for this step, on this data - and it gives you something to point at when the change is questioned later. Price alone tells you what you would save and nothing about what you would lose. A colleague's experience on a different task is about a different distribution, and recency says nothing about fit for a specific step.
why: Price tells you what you would save and nothing about what you would give up to save it.
Correct. An eval on representative production cases showing quality holds for this specific step.
Experience on a different task reflects a different distribution and may not transfer at all.
Release date is not a quality signal for a particular step in your pipeline.

questions.q: Setting reasoning effort per task class rather than globally is preferable because:
opts: It is simpler to configure
Effort is a paid dial and only some task classes convert it into better outcomes
Global settings are unsupported
It guarantees lower cost
questions.exp: Effort is a paid dial and its return varies sharply by task. Multi-step analysis converts it into accuracy; well-specified extraction or classification does not, so a global setting either overspends on the simple classes or underserves the hard ones. Per-class settings capture the benefit where it exists and the saving where it does not. It is more configuration rather than less, which is the honest trade - and it does not guarantee lower cost, since some classes will justify raising it.
why: Per-class configuration is more work than a single global value. The gain is fit rather than simplicity.
Correct. Effort is a paid dial and only some task classes convert it into better outcomes.
Global settings are supported and are the default. The argument is that they fit poorly across mixed workloads.
It does not guarantee lower cost, since some task classes will justify raising effort rather than lowering it.

questions.q: The most defensible way to set a per-run budget cap for an agent is:
opts: A round number chosen by the team
The observed cost distribution of successful runs, with headroom, so caps catch runaway behavior rather than normal work
The cheapest run ever recorded
No cap at all
questions.exp: Derive the cap from the observed cost distribution of successful runs, with headroom. That way it catches runaway behaviour - the loop that never converges - without killing legitimate long runs, which is the failure a round number chosen in a meeting produces in one direction or the other. The cheapest run ever recorded is the worst possible basis, since it would abort the majority of normal work. No cap at all leaves you exposed to exactly the unbounded-loop failure the ceiling exists for.
why: A number chosen without data either aborts legitimate runs or fails to catch runaway ones, and nobody can tell which.
Correct. The observed cost distribution of successful runs plus headroom, so caps catch runaway behaviour rather than normal work.
The cheapest run is an outlier at the wrong end. A cap there would abort most legitimate work.
No cap leaves the unbounded-loop failure entirely unguarded, which is the specific risk a ceiling addresses.

questions.q: Your agent's offline evals look healthy but users report worse results. The most likely gap is:
opts: The evals are too difficult
The eval set no longer reflects the production distribution — real traffic has drifted away from it
Users are mistaken
The model changed silently
questions.exp: The eval set has drifted away from production. Real traffic changes - new use cases, new phrasing, new edge cases - and a fixed suite keeps measuring the distribution it was built for, so it passes confidently while quality falls on what users actually send. The failure is silent by construction: a stale suite does not report that it is stale. Refresh it from production samples periodically, and treat a healthy suite alongside unhappy users as evidence about the suite rather than about the users.
why: Difficulty is not the issue. A hard suite that no longer matches production still measures the wrong thing.
Correct. The eval set no longer reflects the production distribution, so it passes while real traffic has moved on.
Consistent user reports are evidence. Dismissing them discards the most direct signal available.
Silent model changes are rare and would show as a broad shift rather than a gap between evals and reports.

questions.q: An agent reaches the correct final answer, but the trace shows it got there by a route you would not sanction. Your evaluation should:
opts: Score it as a pass, since the output was correct
Score the trajectory as well as the outcome, because a right answer by a wrong route will not generalise
Ignore traces and measure only end-state correctness
Fail every run whose path differs from the reference
questions.exp: Outcome-only scoring rewards luck. An agent that reached the right answer by ignoring a required check, using a tool it should not have, or guessing where it should have verified, will produce a wrong answer on the next input that differs slightly - and outcome metrics will not have warned you. Scoring the trajectory catches that while the run still looks successful. The counterweight matters too: penalising every deviation from a reference path removes the adaptability that justified an agent over a fixed workflow, so the bar is whether the route was legitimate rather than whether it was the expected one.
why: Outcome-only scoring rewards a correct answer reached by luck, and gives no warning before the next input breaks it.
Correct. Score the trajectory as well as the outcome, since a right answer by an illegitimate route will not generalise.
Discarding traces removes the only evidence of how the answer was produced, which is what distinguishes robustness from luck.
Requiring an exact path removes the adaptability that justified using an agent rather than a fixed workflow.

questions.q: The most important property of a regression set used to gate deployments is:
opts: That it is large
That it is representative of real production cases, including known failure modes
That the current system passes all of it
That it changes frequently
questions.exp: Representativeness is what makes the gate meaningful. A suite built from real production cases, including the failure modes you have already seen, tells you whether a change is safe for the traffic you actually have. Size helps only if the cases are representative - a large unrepresentative suite passes confidently while missing everything. A suite the current system passes completely has no discriminating power left, and one that changes frequently cannot be compared across versions, which is the whole point of a regression set.
why: Size without representativeness produces confident passes on cases that do not reflect your traffic.
Correct. Representative of real production cases, including known failure modes, so the gate reflects real risk.
A suite the system already passes entirely has no discriminating power left to detect a regression.
Frequent changes break comparability across versions, which is what a regression set exists to provide.

questions.q: Sampling transcripts for human review remains necessary alongside automated metrics because:
opts: It is required by regulation in all cases
Metrics only measure what you thought to measure; reading transcripts surfaces failure modes you have not encoded
It is cheaper than automation
It replaces the need for evals
questions.exp: Automated metrics measure what you thought to measure. Reading actual transcripts surfaces the failure modes nobody encoded - the agent that answers correctly but rudely, that solves a different problem than asked, that succeeds by a route you would not sanction. Those are invisible to any metric written before you knew they existed, which is precisely why sampling stays in the loop. It is expensive and does not scale, which is why it complements automated evaluation rather than replacing it.
why: Regulatory requirements vary and are not the general reason. The argument is about discovering unknown failure modes.
Correct. Metrics measure only what you thought to measure, and transcripts surface failures nobody encoded.
Human review is considerably more expensive per case than automation. Its value is coverage of the unanticipated.
It complements evals rather than replacing them. Automated evaluation is what makes measurement scale.

questions.q: The right time to build evaluation for an agent workflow is:
opts: After the first production incident
Before meaningful rollout, so changes can be measured from the start
Only if the team has spare capacity
After the prompt stops changing
questions.exp: Before meaningful rollout, so every change afterwards can be measured against a baseline. Building it later means the period when you were learning fastest is the period with no measurement, and you cannot reconstruct whether an early change helped. Waiting for an incident means the first measurement follows the first failure. Waiting for the prompt to stabilise inverts the relationship - evaluation is what tells you a prompt has stabilised, so making it a precondition means it never gets built.
why: Building it after an incident means the first measurement arrives after the first failure, having learned nothing beforehand.
Correct. Before meaningful rollout, so changes can be measured against a baseline from the start.
Treating it as optional means it is never built, since there is always something more urgent.
Evaluation is what tells you a prompt has stabilised, so making stability a precondition is circular.

questions.q: An agent needs to act on behalf of users in two different customer tenants. The critical isolation requirement is:
opts: Separate prompts per tenant
Tenant identity enforced at the data and tool layer, so no request can reach another tenant's data regardless of what the model does
A larger context window per tenant
Running the agent twice
questions.exp: Enforce tenant identity at the data and tool layer, so no request can reach another tenant's data regardless of what the model does. That phrasing is the point: the model is not a security boundary, and any control that depends on it behaving correctly fails the first time it is confused or manipulated. Separate prompts per tenant are a prompt-level convention that an injection can defeat. Server-side enforcement holds even when the model is compromised, which is the only property worth designing for.
why: A prompt is a convention rather than a boundary, and an injection can override it.
Correct. Tenant identity enforced at the data and tool layer, so no request can cross tenants regardless of model behaviour.
Context size has no bearing on whether one tenant's request can reach another's data.
Running twice duplicates work without adding any enforcement of which data each run may access.

questions.q: An agent fleet reads from a shared knowledge store that any team can write to. The main governance risk is:
opts: Storage cost
Poisoned or unreviewed content silently steering every agent that reads it
Slower retrieval
Duplicate documents
questions.exp: Unreviewed content in a shared store steers every agent that reads it, which makes it both a quality risk and an injection vector - text placed there is retrieved into context and can be crafted to read as instruction. The scale is what makes it serious: one bad document affects every agent, silently, and nothing in any output indicates the source was unreviewed. Governance here means write controls, review, and provenance tracking. Storage cost and duplicate documents are operational annoyances by comparison.
why: Storage is cheap and is not the governance concern. The risk is what unreviewed content does to every reader.
Correct. Poisoned or unreviewed content silently steers every agent that reads it, at scale and without signal.
Retrieval speed is a performance property rather than a governance risk.
Duplicates cause redundancy. Unreviewed or malicious content causes wrong behaviour across the fleet.

questions.q: Agents act on behalf of users with differing permissions. The correct model is:
opts: Give the agent broad service credentials for simplicity
Have the agent act with the requesting user's effective permissions, enforced server-side
Ask the agent to check permissions itself in the prompt
Grant permissions per tool regardless of user
questions.exp: The agent should act with the requesting user's effective permissions, enforced server-side. That is the only model where a confused or manipulated agent cannot exceed what the user could have done themselves - the boundary holds independently of the model's behaviour. Broad service credentials make every request as powerful as the most privileged user, which is the standard confused-deputy failure. Asking the agent to check permissions itself puts the control inside the thing being controlled.
why: Broad service credentials make every request as powerful as the most privileged user, which is a confused-deputy failure.
Correct. The agent acts with the requesting user's effective permissions, enforced server-side.
A prompt instruction places the control inside the component being controlled, which an injection can defeat.
Per-tool permissions ignoring the user mean any user reaches whatever that tool can reach.

questions.q: Audit requirements for an agent that takes consequential actions should include:
opts: The final output only
Who requested it, what the agent did, which tools ran with which inputs, and what approvals were given
Token counts only
Nothing, since actions are automated
questions.exp: An audit trail has to answer who asked, what was done, with what inputs, and who approved it. Each part is needed for a different question - accountability, reconstruction, root cause, and authorisation - and a trail missing any one of them fails exactly when it is needed. Recording only the final output tells you what happened without telling you why or on whose authority. Token counts are cost data. The idea that automated actions need no audit inverts the requirement, since automation is what makes reconstruction impossible without records.
why: The final output shows the result without showing who asked, what ran, or on whose authority.
Correct. Requester, actions taken, tools and inputs, and approvals - each answering a different audit question.
Token counts are cost data and say nothing about what was done or authorised.
Automation increases the need for audit, since without records there is no way to reconstruct what happened.

questions.q: A customer asks whether an agent can be given autonomous authority to issue refunds. The right answer is:
opts: Yes, if the prompt says to be careful
It depends on defined limits, approval thresholds, and audit — with irreversible or high-value actions gated by a human
No, agents can never take actions
Yes, if the model is capable enough
questions.exp: The honest answer is conditional. Bounded autonomy works with defined limits, approval thresholds and audit - small refunds automatically, larger ones gated by a person - and that structure is what makes it defensible rather than the model's capability. Saying yes because the prompt asks for care mistakes an instruction for a control. Saying no on principle is wrong too, since agents take actions routinely and refusing all of it forgoes real value. Capability is the least relevant factor: a more capable model does not change who is accountable.
why: An instruction to be careful is not a limit. Nothing enforces it and nothing bounds the outcome.
Correct. Defined limits, approval thresholds and audit, with irreversible or high-value actions gated by a human.
Agents take consequential actions routinely under appropriate controls. A blanket no forgoes real value.
Capability does not change accountability or the need for limits. A more capable model acts wrongly more effectively.

questions.q: A high-volume agent step is latency-bound rather than cost-bound. The most effective first change is:
opts: Move it to the strongest available model
Move it to a faster model tier and stream, then re-measure before doing anything more elaborate
Add more retries
Increase the reasoning effort
questions.exp: Move it to a faster tier, stream, and re-measure before doing anything more elaborate. That is the change that addresses the actual constraint, and re-measuring is what stops you optimising past the point where latency stopped being the bottleneck. The other options all push the wrong way: a stronger model and higher reasoning effort both increase latency in exchange for capability the step may not need, and retries add latency by definition. Fix the binding constraint first, then look again.
why: A stronger model generally increases latency, which is the constraint you are trying to relieve.
Correct. A faster tier with streaming, then re-measure before anything more elaborate.
Retries add latency by definition and address failure rather than speed.
More reasoning effort deepens thinking and lengthens responses, both of which increase latency.

questions.q: An agent needs a credential to call an internal system. The safest handling is:
opts: Put the credential in the system prompt so the agent can use it
Keep the credential in the execution environment behind a tool, so the model never sees the secret itself
Let the agent read it from a shared document
Embed it in the tool description
questions.exp: Keep the credential in the execution environment behind a tool, so the model never sees it. The model produces a tool call; your code holds the secret and makes the authenticated request. That way nothing the model outputs, and nothing an injection persuades it to output, can reveal the credential. Putting it in the system prompt is the worst option because prompts persist in conversation history and traces, which turns a transient secret into a stored one across every logging and observability system it touches.
why: Prompts persist in conversation history and traces, so this turns a secret into a stored record across every system that logs.
Correct. The credential stays in the execution environment behind a tool, so the model never sees the secret itself.
A shared document is another place the secret is stored and readable, and the model still ends up handling it.
Tool descriptions are sent to the model like any other prompt content, so this exposes it just as directly.

questions.q: A financial trading intelligence system uses 8 specialized subagents. Why is a centralized Blackboard Pattern superior to peer-to-peer message passing?
opts: It decouples agent communication through a structured shared state store, preventing exponential token bloat and context contamination
It translates all financial data into physical paper trading tickets
It requires only a single CPU core to run all agents
It eliminates the need for database storage
questions.exp: A shared state store decouples the agents from each other. With peer-to-peer messaging every agent accumulates every other agent's context, so token consumption grows with the square of the fleet and each agent's reasoning is contaminated by material it did not need. A blackboard means agents read and write structured state instead of talking, so the growth is linear and each one sees only what it looks up. The trade is a coordination point you must design carefully - the blackboard's schema becomes the contract every agent depends on.
why: Correct. A structured shared state store decouples communication, keeping token growth linear and contexts uncontaminated.
The pattern concerns how agents share state in software. It has no physical component.
Compute requirements follow the work being done rather than the coordination pattern chosen.
A blackboard is typically backed by storage rather than replacing it.

questions.q: An autonomous agent reads incoming vendor invoices and executes payment database mutations. How should the architecture prevent Indirect Prompt Injection?
opts: Treat invoice text as untrusted data, enforce strict payment authorization limits, and require out-of-band multi-factor human approval for disbursements
Trust all invoice instructions if they contain the word 'URGENT'
Disable all company accounts payable operations permanently
Set model temperature to 1.0 to randomize payments
questions.exp: Invoice text arrives from outside your organisation, so it is untrusted input that happens to be shaped like a document - and an attacker who can send you an invoice can put text in it. Three controls stack here: treat the content as data rather than instruction, cap what any single authorisation can move, and require human approval out of band for disbursement. The out-of-band part matters, because an approval that flows through the same compromised channel as the request approves whatever the attacker asked for.
why: Correct. Invoice text is untrusted data, with authorisation limits and out-of-band human approval bounding what any injection could achieve.
Urgency markers are trivially forged and are a standard social-engineering lever rather than a trust signal.
Shutting down the business function avoids the risk by abandoning the capability entirely.
Sampling parameters do not affect safety, and current models reject them regardless.

questions.q: When configuring OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions for Claude API calls, what standard span attributes must be recorded?
opts: `gen_ai.system: 'anthropic'`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens`, and `gen_ai.usage.completion_tokens`
Raw unencrypted employee passwords and credit card numbers
Only the HTTP 200 status code with zero model metadata
A generic text string saying 'success'
questions.exp: The conventions exist so traces from different systems can be queried the same way: which provider, which model, and how many tokens in and out. Recording those consistently is what lets you attribute cost, spot a regression after a model change, and compare across services without bespoke parsing per team. The discipline worth carrying is what does *not* belong in a span - traces are widely readable and long-lived, so credentials and personal data placed there become a durable exposure with weaker access controls than the system they came from.
why: Correct. Provider, model, and token counts in and out - the standard attributes that make traces comparable and cost attributable.
Credentials and payment data must never enter traces, which are widely readable and long-lived.
A status code alone tells you the call succeeded and nothing about which model ran or what it cost.
An unstructured success string cannot be aggregated, filtered or compared across services.

questions.q: An enterprise customer support fleet experiences sudden CRM database latency spikes. What Circuit Breaker pattern prevents thread pool exhaustion?
opts: Trip the circuit breaker to OPEN after consecutive timeouts, immediately serving cached customer data without waiting for network timeouts
Increase the network timeout to 60 minutes per request
Spam 5,000 concurrent retry requests every second
Delete the customer CRM database
questions.exp: When a dependency slows down, the danger is not the failure itself but the queue behind it: every waiting request holds a thread, and a slow dependency exhausts the pool, taking down requests that had nothing to do with it. Tripping the breaker open after consecutive timeouts fails fast instead of waiting, and serving cached data keeps the system useful while the dependency recovers. The half-open probe afterwards is what lets it close again without a thundering wave of retries.
why: Correct. Trip open after consecutive timeouts and fail fast on cached data, so waiting requests stop consuming threads.
A longer timeout makes exhaustion worse, since each request holds its thread for longer.
Aggressive retries add load to a dependency that is already saturated, extending the outage.
Removing the dependency destroys the data the system exists to serve.

questions.q: A regulated customer asks how Anthropic decides which safeguards a frontier model requires. The accurate answer is:
opts: A published, tiered framework in which crossing a defined capability threshold requires stronger security and deployment safeguards
Safeguards are fixed when a model launches and do not escalate
Each deployment negotiates its own safeguards privately with no published standard
Safeguards depend on the customer's contract tier rather than the model
questions.exp: Anthropic publishes a tiered responsible-scaling framework: models are evaluated against defined capability thresholds, and crossing one triggers a stronger set of security and deployment requirements rather than a private judgement call. For an architect answering a regulated customer, two properties matter more than the tier numbers. It is capability-triggered, so it does not vary by contract or deployment surface, and it is public, so it can be cited in a compliance review rather than paraphrased. Point at the published policy for the current thresholds; those are updated as the framework evolves, which is exactly why quoting remembered figures into an audit response is unsafe.
why: Correct. Tiered and threshold-driven, escalating as measured capability crosses defined levels, and published so a customer can verify it.
The framework exists specifically to escalate as capability grows, so a fixed-at-launch description is backwards.
There is a published standard. Describing it as privately negotiated understates a public commitment and would not survive a compliance review.
Requirements follow the model's assessed capability, not what a customer is paying for. That distinction is the point of the framework.

questions.q: In a production multi-agent system, how do Architects prevent deadlocks between interdependent subagents?
opts: Enforce a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) task dependency structure and apply strict wall-clock iteration timeouts on all agent loops
Let agents run in circular loops indefinitely until memory runs out
Disable all inter-agent communication completely
Force all agents to share a single unencrypted global variable
questions.exp: Two mechanisms, one structural and one temporal. A directed acyclic dependency graph makes circular waits impossible by construction - if the dependencies cannot form a cycle, agents cannot wait on each other indefinitely. Wall-clock timeouts then catch what the structure cannot: a stalled external dependency, or an agent that is simply not converging. Together they cover both the design-time and run-time cases. Disabling communication entirely avoids deadlock by removing coordination, which is a different system rather than a fix.
why: Correct. A DAG dependency structure makes circular waits impossible, and wall-clock timeouts catch stalls the structure cannot.
Unbounded circular loops are the deadlock being described rather than a response to it.
Removing coordination avoids deadlock by removing the collaboration that justified a multi-agent design.
Shared mutable state without synchronisation adds race conditions on top of the deadlock risk.

questions.q: When running untrusted agent-generated Python code in production, which containerization technology provides strong virtualization security?
opts: gVisor or Firecracker microVMs with dedicated guest kernels and restricted syscall interception
Running code directly on the bare-metal production host as root
An unsandboxed eval() statement inside a public Node.js Express server
Saving Python files directly to the Windows Desktop folder
questions.exp: Model-generated code is untrusted code, and it needs a boundary that holds even when the code is actively hostile. A microVM or a kernel-isolating sandbox gives each execution its own kernel surface and intercepts syscalls, so an escape has to defeat virtualisation rather than a language-level guard. That distinction is the point - process-level sandboxes inside a shared runtime have a much larger attack surface. Pair it with egress restriction, because code that cannot reach the network cannot exfiltrate whatever it does read.
why: Correct. MicroVMs or kernel-isolating sandboxes give each execution its own kernel surface and intercept syscalls.
Running untrusted code as root on a production host removes every boundary at once.
Unsandboxed evaluation inside a public server is remote code execution by design.
Writing files to a desktop folder is not isolation and provides no containment of any kind.

questions.q: How should a multi-tenant enterprise SaaS platform track token consumption and API billing across 500 enterprise customers?
opts: Attach `metadata: { 'tenant_id': orgId, 'user_id': userId }` to every API request for automated usage aggregation in logs and dashboards
Hardcode each customer's credit card number in the prompt text
Create a brand new Anthropic account for every customer query
Ask customers to self-report their token counts on honor system
questions.exp: Attach tenant and user identifiers as request metadata so usage aggregates automatically. That gives you per-customer attribution without threading accounting through your application logic, and it is what makes both billing and anomaly detection possible - a single tenant's runaway job is visible immediately rather than buried in a total. The alternative approaches all fail differently: separate accounts per query is unmanageable at 500 customers, self-reporting is not measurement, and credentials in prompt text is a data-handling failure.
why: Correct. Identifiers attached as request metadata give automatic per-tenant attribution for both billing and anomaly detection.
Payment details must never appear in prompt text, which is stored in conversation history and traces.
An account per query is unmanageable at this scale and fragments usage data beyond use.
Self-reporting is not measurement, and it cannot detect a runaway job in anyone's account.

questions.q: In a mission-critical banking application, what is the recommended fallback cascade sequence when Claude Sonnet 5 encounters an outage?
opts: Retry with exponential backoff -> Fallback to Claude Haiku 4.5 -> Fallback to static rule-based templates -> Graceful human escalation
Crash the entire banking application immediately
Switch all users to random Wikipedia articles
Reboot the cloud data center hardware
questions.exp: Each rung degrades a little further and covers a failure the one above cannot. Backoff handles transients. A faster, cheaper tier keeps the service intelligent when the primary is unavailable. Static templates keep it responding when no model is reachable. Human escalation covers what templates cannot answer. In a banking context that ordering matters more than elsewhere, because silently degrading to a weaker answer without acknowledging it is worse than a clear handoff - the user needs to know what kind of answer they are getting.
why: Correct. Backoff, then a faster tier, then static templates, then human escalation - each rung covering what the one above cannot.
Crashing a banking application converts a dependency outage into a total service failure.
Serving unrelated content is worse than an error, since users cannot tell it is not an answer.
Infrastructure restarts are not an application-level response to an upstream outage.

questions.q: Why should high-assurance enterprise deployments maintain a version-controlled Golden Evaluation Dataset of 500+ challenging scenarios?
opts: To run automated regression tests before deploying any prompt, tool schema, or model version update to production
To fill up excess cloud storage quotas
To train competitor AI models
To comply with website cookie banner regulations
questions.exp: A version-controlled evaluation set is what makes any change to a production agent measurable: prompt edits, tool schema changes, and model version updates all alter behaviour, and without a fixed baseline you cannot tell an improvement from a regression. Version control matters as much as the content, because a set that drifts silently cannot be compared across releases. Challenging scenarios are the point too - a suite of easy cases passes everything and discriminates nothing.
why: Correct. Automated regression testing before any prompt, tool schema, or model version change reaches production.
Storage is incidental. The value is a fixed baseline that makes behaviour changes measurable.
Evaluation sets exist to measure your own system rather than to serve anyone else.
Cookie regulation is unrelated to evaluating agent behaviour.

questions.q: Why do autonomous agent loops require hard iteration caps and session spend ceilings in production?
opts: To prevent runaway loops from consuming infinite tokens and budget during unexpected edge-case failures
Because cloud servers automatically shut down after 5 loops
Because Anthropic limits every account to 10 total tool calls
Because loops increase computer monitor brightness
questions.exp: An autonomous loop decides how long to continue, so without an external bound the failure mode is unbounded rather than merely bad. An edge case that prevents convergence will keep the loop running and spending, and nothing inside the loop is positioned to notice. Caps convert an open-ended risk into a known worst case, which is what makes autonomy operationally acceptable. Pair them with an escalation path, because a cap that simply stops leaves the work in an undefined state rather than a recoverable one.
why: Correct. They convert an unbounded failure into a known worst case when an edge case prevents convergence.
No such platform limit exists. The bound has to come from your own design.
There is no fixed tool-call cap of that kind. Limits are yours to set.
Hardware has no relationship to loop control.

questions.q: What is the primary security vulnerability when an agent is given access to both internal confidential files and public web browsing tools?
opts: Indirect prompt injection from public web pages instructing the agent to exfiltrate confidential internal context to an attacker's server
The agent's output text automatically turning into French
The computer monitor screen turning off
The API key expiring after 5 minutes
questions.exp: The combination is the vulnerability. Browsing alone is low-risk and file access alone is controlled; joining them creates a path from attacker-controlled text to your confidential data, because a web page can carry instructions telling the agent to read internal context and send it somewhere. This is why capability combinations deserve their own review - each tool passed its individual assessment. The mitigations are structural: isolate fetched content, restrict which tools are reachable while browsing, and filter egress.
why: Correct. Injection from public pages instructing the agent to exfiltrate internal context - a risk created by combining the two capabilities.
Language drift is not a security concern and is not what injection produces.
Display behaviour has nothing to do with an agent's data access.
